name: lsmod
summary: List the kernel modules (drivers) currently loaded.
compat: Reads /proc/modules; no root needed. Drivers built into the kernel (=y in the config) never appear here, even though they are active. Containers and WSL show the host or WSL kernel's modules.

examples.title: Is my module loaded?
examples.explain: Module names use underscores in lsmod even if the file name has dashes.
examples.output: Columns: Module, Size (bytes), 'Used by' count and the modules using it. A non-zero count means it cannot be removed until users go away.

examples.title: List all loaded modules
examples.explain: Shows every module loaded right now, newest first.

name: modinfo
summary: Show a kernel module's metadata: file path, description, license, parameters, aliases.
compat: Given a name, looks under /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/; given a path, reads that .ko file. No root needed.

examples.title: Show metadata of an installed module
examples.explain: Try a common one such as modinfo usbcore or modinfo loop (if built as a module).
examples.output: filename = the .ko on disk; parm = parameters you can set; alias = device IDs that auto-load it; vermagic = kernel version it was built for. 'not found' means it is not installed as a module (maybe built in, or for another kernel).

examples.title: Inspect a module file you built
examples.explain: Check vermagic matches uname -r before trying to load it; a mismatch causes 'Invalid module format'.

examples.title: Show only one field
examples.explain: -F prints a single field, handy in scripts.

name: modprobe
summary: Load or unload an installed kernel module together with its dependencies.
compat: Works with modules installed under /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/ (after depmod). For a .ko in your build directory, use insmod. Secure Boot may refuse unsigned modules.

examples.title: Preview what would be loaded
examples.explain: Dry run (inspect-first): prints the insmod steps, including dependencies, without loading anything.

examples.title: Load a module
examples.explain: Loads dependencies first. Check dmesg afterwards for the driver's messages.
examples.warning: Runs kernel code as root. A buggy or wrong module can freeze or crash the whole machine; practise on a VM or test board, and save your work first.

examples.title: Unload a module
examples.explain: Fails with 'in use' if something still uses it (see lsmod's Used by column).
examples.warning: Removing a driver in use (disk, network, display, input) can cut off storage, connectivity or your session. Only unload modules you loaded for testing.

name: insmod
summary: Load a specific .ko file, typically your own freshly built driver.
compat: insmod does not load dependencies (modprobe does). The .ko must be built against the running kernel's headers: check modinfo -F vermagic vs uname -r.

examples.title: Load your module with a parameter
examples.explain: Then check sudo dmesg | tail for your init function's messages and lsmod | grep <module>.
examples.warning: Your module runs in the kernel with no protection: a NULL pointer or infinite loop can oops, hang or panic the system. Use a VM or test board, not the machine you depend on.
examples.output: 'Invalid module format' = built for another kernel version/architecture; 'File exists' = already loaded; 'Unknown symbol' (see dmesg) = missing dependency or license mismatch; 'Operation not permitted' = not root or Secure Boot lockdown.

name: rmmod
summary: Unload a kernel module by name.
compat: Takes the module name (as shown by lsmod), not the .ko path, although kmod also accepts a path.

examples.title: Unload your test module
examples.explain: Calls your module's exit function; check dmesg for its messages.
examples.warning: Only unload modules you loaded for testing. Removing drivers for hardware in use can break storage, network or input. 'Module is in use' means you must close its users first.

name: udevadm
summary: Watch device add/remove events and see the attributes udev rules can match.

install.note: Minimal embedded systems may use mdev (BusyBox) or a static /dev instead of udev.

compat: Device events are not available in most containers or WSL without extra setup.

examples.title: Watch device events while plugging hardware
examples.explain: Plug in a USB-serial adapter and see the events with properties such as DEVNAME=/dev/ttyUSB0. Ctrl+C stops.

examples.title: Show attributes for writing a udev rule
examples.explain: <device> like /dev/ttyUSB0. Lists ATTRS{idVendor}, ATTRS{idProduct}, ATTRS{serial} up the parent chain, which rules can match on.
options: Print attributes of the device and its parents
